hero.titleLine2: queried at native SQL index speed.
hero.lede: Give every tenant their own fields, then filter them like first-class columns. No separate search cluster. No EAV join swamp. Just MySQL or MariaDB, doing an index scan on data you never declared at migration time.

mirror.title: One row of truth, mirrored into an index.
mirror.lede: The complete JSON payload is always the system of record. Fields you mark filterable are additionally mirrored into typed, indexed slot columns on a 1:1 extension page — so a filter reads a real index instead of scanning JSON. Edit the payload below and write it.

joins.title: Every EAV condition is another self-join.
joins.lede: The classic attribute table makes a narrower question cost more, because each filtered attribute needs its own join and the intermediate result has to be carried through all of them. StarDust joins once per indexed page the model's fields occupy, not once per condition — so when those fields share a page, it is one join however many conditions you stack on it.

lifecycle.title: Filterable is a promise the daemons keep, not an instant.
lifecycle.lede: This is the behaviour that trips up nearly everyone, so it gets its own section rather than a footnote. Marking a field filterable records an intention and returns immediately — two background daemons then do the work that makes filtering actually possible.

daemons.title: Four daemons. No broker between them.
daemons.lede: They never talk to each other directly — the database is the only coordination point, with claims taken under FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and the Watcher's singleton held by advisory lock. Run more Reconcilers, Liberators, and Chroniclers for throughput — only the Watcher stays one apiece.

status.title: Whether you should actually use this.
status.lede: The current release is 0.3.0-alpha.1 — a ground-up rewrite (Vertical Schema Partitioning) of the legacy 0.2.x line, sharing no API with it. It hasn't reached 1.0, and the public API may still change before 0.3.0. Everything below is implemented and covered by the test suite.

start.title: Five minutes, one command.
start.lede: Brings up MySQL, bootstraps the schema, seeds a sample model, runs a filtered query, and starts all four daemons.

good.heading: a good fit if
items: You need user-defined or per-tenant dynamic fields that are still filterable at native index speed, without standing up a search cluster.
You already run MySQL 8.0.13+, Percona, or MariaDB 10.11+ — either deployment mode works, persistent daemons or a scheduled tick.
You want a framework-neutral engine you drop in via Composer. No ORM, no query builder, nothing pulled into your app.
You can tolerate a newly filterable field becoming queryable shortly after the fact rather than instantly.

bad.heading: probably not a fit if
items: MariaDB 10.6 or older, or MySQL 5.7 and older. Both are actively rejected at boot — CI keeps a job that expects the suite to fail on a server below the floor.
Strong read-after-write consistency on filters immediately after a retype or promotion. The field serves from JSON until its backfill lands.
Full-text, fuzzy, or substring search. The default driver ships exact match, comparison, range, set membership, and anchored prefix — nothing else.
Page numbers, jump-to-page, or a total result count. Reads are cursor-paginated and forward-sequential, deliberately.

joinSwamp.eavNote: Each condition adds a join, and the intermediate result has to be carried through all of them — so asking a narrower question costs strictly more.
joinSwamp.sdHead: StarDust — one join per page, not per condition
joinSwamp.sdNote: With the model's fields on one page, every condition is another predicate on the same indexed row. Narrower question, less work — the way an index is supposed to behave.
joinSwamp.factorOne: more rows touched by EAV at {count} condition
joinSwamp.factorMany: more rows touched by EAV at {count} conditions
joinSwamp.disclaimer: An illustrative cost model of join fan-out — not a benchmark. The shape is what matters: EAV grows with the number of conditions, StarDust does not. Measure your own workload before quoting a number.

acts.act0Blurb: The call recorded an intention and came back immediately. Nothing has been indexed. This is the state people file bugs about.
acts.act1Blurb: No page had a free indexed int slot, so the Watcher provisions one. A page carries exactly the columns it indexes, four of every type family, so the three spare int columns are what let the next few promotions skip this step. It provisions capacity and nothing else — claiming a slot is not its job, so the field is still unmapped when this tick ends.
acts.act2Title: the Reconciler claims the slot and backfills
acts.act2Blurb: The Reconciler reserves the slot as backfilling, then copies every existing entry’s value out of JSON into the slot column in chunks, checkpointing after each one.
acts.act3Blurb: The last chunk promotes the slot and bumps the schema version. The identical read() call that was throwing a minute ago now returns rows.

daemonBoard.legend: Nothing here is a message queue. Every arrow is a connection to the database.
daemonBoard.watcherRole: Provisions indexed pages before capacity runs out.
daemonBoard.reconcilerRole: Drains six work sources under SKIP LOCKED.
daemonBoard.liberatorRole: Sweeps tombstoned slots back to free, so capacity is reused.
daemonBoard.chroniclerRole: Streams CSV/JSON export artifacts straight to disk.
daemonBoard.coreSub: sole coordination point — no broker, no daemon-to-daemon RPC
